title: NPM Link and the CTO of a Two-Person Startup: a Horror Story
description: One day, I decided my team deserved a proper package architecture. I had no idea the kind of chaos I was about to unleash.
author: Daniel Sanchez

paragraphs.content: Where the Chaos Began
`Coding Flavour` is a tiny software team made up of two developers and a designer, all working toward the same goal: building products for ourselves.
Developers have come and gone over time, but the core team has remained the same since the beginning.

Inside `Coding Flavour`, I naturally ended up taking the role of lead developer. In practice, that means I handle most of the technical decisions, mostly because I have the most experience in the team. For context, my teammate had only been programming for about two years at that point. Still a baby.
Most of the technical responsibility falls on me, but I always try to make decisions together with the rest of the team.
From the very beginning, even without having a clear product, our strategy was simple: build as many POCs as possible and see what sticks.
Any random idea that crossed our minds would go through a bit of brainstorming and eventually become a small prototype.
At some point, when you're trying to lead projects like this, you inevitably start making questionable decisions:

items: Should I sacrifice quality for development speed?
Do I really need rate limiting for my total user base of one person?

paragraphs.content: And this kind of thinking never comes alone. Nobody starts using `NextJS` for absolutely everything without also making several other terrible architectural decisions along the way.

items: Bugs spreading across multiple projects, with the fix buried somewhere else
The same components rewritten over and over again with tiny meaningless variations

paragraphs.content: Eventually, completely exhausted from weird architectures and growing technical debt, I decided to take matters into my own hands.
So, in an attempt to help us move faster, I proposed creating several shared utility packages, all fully tested and designed to maximize code reuse and stability.
What could possibly go wrong?
That's when the real nightmare started: realizing how difficult it is to maintain an architecture you never fully planned properly.
The first thing we did was analyze all our repositories and start extracting everything into shared packages:
Just like that, we went from copying the same code thirty times to having thirty repositories installing thirty different internal tools.
The beginning of chaos.
After that, we had to make an important decision: how were we actually going to consume these packages?

We didn't want to publish our libraries publicly on NPM, and we definitely didn't have the budget for paid solutions like private NPM registries. And honestly, at that point I didn't even fully understand what I wanted yet, so I never stopped to explore tools like `Verdaccio`.
So what was the next *easiest* solution? `npm link`, of course.
And with that decision, the real suffering began.

Personally, as someone with a decent amount of development experience, the process was mostly just *annoying*. But now imagine trying to explain all of this to less experienced developers, like my teammates at `Coding Flavour`.

"Oh, you want to build a simple TODO app as a POC? Sure. First install the project. Then link `@coding-flavour/icons` inside `@coding-flavour/styles`. After that, go into `@coding-flavour/common` and link both `@coding-flavour/styles` and `@coding-flavour/icons`. And don't forget to link all three of them inside your actual project too."
A completely unreasonable amount of complexity for a beginner developer who just wants to write some code and prototype an idea.
Links that break if you create them in the wrong order. Random packages unlinking themselves. Trying to figure out which project is now pointing somewhere it shouldn't.

You accidentally linked `common` without updating `styles`, and now you somehow have two completely different versions of the same package: your local changes, and the stale linked copy sitting inside `node_modules` refusing to update.
And of course, the funniest part: manually deleting broken symlinks from the global `npm` directory because the link is pointing to an outdated version and refuses to refresh properly.

At some point, this entire setup stops being viable when you're the person responsible for the architecture and the entire team depends on understanding weird `npm` internals just to debug basic problems.
Thanks to all these *brilliant* ideas, I had successfully dragged the entire team into a dependency nightmare entirely created by me.
While all of this was happening, I was also changing jobs in real life, which came with a lot of new learning opportunities.
At this new company, I ended up working on testing infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, and even data analysis. That also gave me access to many internal tools developed by the company itself.

One of those tools was `Artifactory`: a package management platform built around `JFrog`, acting as a middleware layer between NPM and the final consumer installation process. It cached secure versions of NPM packages to help avoid supply chain and security issues, among many other things.

But what really caught my attention was the fact that it could also host private company packages. Since it already operated on top of a filesystem-based architecture, publishing and serving your own packages was apparently fairly straightforward.
The moment I saw it, my brain immediately went: "Wait... this solves literally **ALL** my problems!!"
And naturally, five minutes later I was already opening VSCode thinking about building my own version.

Jokes aside, maybe this wasn't the perfect solution, but creating a lightweight custom registry sounded infinitely simpler than manually managing symlinks across half a dozen packages while screen-sharing with someone trying to debug why their dependencies had exploded again.
A new goal was born: I wanted my teammates to install private packages as effortlessly as if they came directly from NPM. Something as simple as `npm install @coding-flavour/logger` should just work.
And with that small shift in mindset and architecture, the journey of building our own custom `Artifactory` registry officially began.
